{{short description|Maximal independent set of the matroid}}
In mathematics, a '''basis''' of a [[matroid]] is a [[maximal independent set]] of the matroid—that is, an independent set that is not contained in any other independent set.

== Examples ==
As an example, consider the matroid over the ground-set '''R'''<sup>2</sup> (the vectors in the two-dimensional Euclidean plane), with the following independent sets:   {{block indent|{  {},  {(0,1)},  {(2,0)},    {(0,1),(2,0)},   {(0,3)},   {(0,3),(2,0)}  }. }}It has two bases, which are the sets  {(0,1),(2,0)} ,  {(0,3),(2,0)}. These are the only independent sets that are maximal under inclusion.

The basis has a specialized name in several specialized kinds of matroids:<ref>{{Cite web|last=Ardila|first=Federico|date=2007|title=Matroids, lecture 3|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L7U1k_urI0U|url-status=live|website=youtube|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200214051519/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L7U1k_urI0U |archive-date=2020-02-14 }}</ref>

* In a [[graphic matroid]], where the independent sets are the forests, the bases are called the ''[[spanning forest]]s'' of the graph. 
* In a [[transversal matroid]], where the independent sets are endpoints of matchings in a given [[bipartite graph]], the bases are called ''transversals''. 
* In a [[linear matroid]], where the independent sets are the [[Linear independence|linearly-independent]] sets of vectors in a given vector-space, the bases are just called ''bases'' of the vector space.  Hence, the concept of basis of a matroid generalizes the concept of [[Basis (linear algebra)|basis from linear algebra]].  
*In a [[uniform matroid]], where the independent sets are all sets with cardinality at most ''k'' (for some integer ''k''), the bases are all sets with cardinality exactly ''k''.  
*In a [[partition matroid]], where elements are partitioned into categories and the independent sets are all sets containing at most ''k<sub>c</sub>'' elements from each category ''c,'' the bases are all sets which contain exactly ''k<sub>c</sub>'' elements from category ''c''.  
*In a [[free matroid]], where all subsets of the ground-set ''E'' are independent, the unique basis is ''E.''

== Properties ==

=== Exchange ===
All matroids satisfy the following properties, for any two distinct bases <math>A</math> and <math>B</math>:<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|date=2016-01-01|title=An infinite family of excluded minors for strong base-orderability|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0024379515005935|journal=Linear Algebra and Its Applications|language=en|volume=488|pages=396–429|arxiv=1507.05521|doi=10.1016/j.laa.2015.09.055|issn=0024-3795 |last1=Bonin|first1=Joseph E.|last2=Savitsky|first2=Thomas J.|s2cid=119161534}}
*{{cite web |author=Joseph E. Bonin |author2=Thomas J. Savitsky |date=April 2016 |title=Excluded Minors for (Strongly) Base-Orderable Matroids |website= |url=https://blogs.gwu.edu/jbonin/files/2016/04/BaseOrderable-rjuvq2.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pipoFmeDWIs|title = Matroids Lecture 2: Bases|website = [[YouTube]]| date=16 August 2020 }}</ref>

* '''Basis-exchange property''': if <math>a\in A\setminus B</math>, then there exists an element <math>b\in B\setminus A</math> such that <math>(A \setminus \{ a \}) \cup \{b\}</math> is a basis. 
* '''Symmetric basis-exchange property''': if <math>a\in A\setminus B</math>, then there exists an element <math>b\in B\setminus A</math> such that both <math>(A \setminus \{ a \}) \cup \{b\}</math> and <math>(B \setminus \{ b \}) \cup \{a\}</math> are bases. Brualdi<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last=Brualdi|first=Richard A.|date=1969-08-01|title=Comments on bases in dependence structures|journal=Bulletin of the Australian Mathematical Society|language=en|volume=1|issue=2|pages=161–167|doi=10.1017/S000497270004140X|issn=1755-1633|doi-access=free}}</ref> showed that it is in fact equivalent to the basis-exchange property. 
* '''Multiple symmetric basis-exchange property''':   if <math>X\subseteq A\setminus B</math>, then there exists a subset <math>Y\subseteq  B\setminus A</math> such that both <math>(A \setminus X) \cup Y</math> and <math>(B \setminus Y) \cup X</math> are bases. Brylawski, Greene, and Woodall, showed (independently) that it is in fact equivalent to the basis-exchange property. 
* '''Bijective basis-exchange property''': There is a bijection ''<math>f</math>'' from ''<math>A</math>'' to <math>B</math>, such that for every <math>a\in A\setminus B</math>, <math>(A \setminus \{ a \}) \cup \{f(a)\}</math> is a basis. Brualdi<ref name=":1" /> showed that it is equivalent to the basis-exchange property. 
*'''Partition basis-exchange property''': For each partition <math>(A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_m)</math> of ''<math>A</math>'' into ''m'' parts, there exists a partition <math>(B_1, B_2, \ldots, B_m)</math> of <math>B</math> into ''m'' parts, such that for every <math>i\in[m]</math>, <math>(A \setminus A_i) \cup B_i</math> is a basis.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Greene|first1=Curtis|last2=Magnanti|first2=Thomas L.|date=1975-11-01|title=Some Abstract Pivot Algorithms|url=https://epubs.siam.org/doi/pdf/10.1137/0129045|journal=SIAM Journal on Applied Mathematics|language=en-US|volume=29|issue=3|pages=530–539|doi=10.1137/0129045|issn=0036-1399|hdl=1721.1/5113|hdl-access=free}}</ref>

However, a basis-exchange property that is ''both'' symmetric ''and'' bijective is not satisfied by all matroids: it is satisfied only by [[base-orderable matroid]]s.

In general, in the symmetric basis-exchange property, the element <math>b\in B\setminus A</math> need not be unique. [[Regular matroid]]s have the '''unique exchange property''', meaning that for ''some'' <math>a\in A\setminus B</math>, the corresponding ''b'' is unique.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=McGuinness|first=Sean|date=2014-07-01|title=A base exchange property for regular matroids|journal=Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B|language=en|volume=107|pages=42–77|doi=10.1016/j.jctb.2014.02.004|issn=0095-8956|doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== Cardinality ===
It follows from the basis exchange property that no member of <math>\mathcal{B}</math> can be a proper subset of another.

Moreover, all bases of a given matroid have the same cardinality. In a linear matroid, the cardinality of all bases is called the [[Dimension (vector space)|dimension]] of the vector space.

===Neil  White's conjecture ===
It is conjectured that all matroids satisfy the following property:<ref name=":0" /> For every integer ''t'' ≥ 1'','' If '''B''' and '''B'''' are two ''t''-tuples of bases with the same multi-set union, then there is a sequence of symmetric exchanges that transforms '''B''' to '''B''''.

== Characterization ==
The bases of a matroid characterize the matroid completely: a set is independent if and only if it is a subset of a basis. Moreover, one may define a matroid <math>M</math> to be a pair <math>(E,\mathcal{B})</math>, where <math>E</math> is the ground-set and <math>\mathcal{B}</math> is a collection of subsets of <math>E</math>, called "bases", with the following properties:<ref name="w7-9">{{citation|last=Welsh|first=D. J. A.|title=Matroid Theory|volume=8|year=1976|series=L.M.S. Monographs|publisher=Academic Press|isbn=978-0-12-744050-7|zbl=0343.05002}}. Section 1.2, "Axiom Systems for a Matroid", pp. 7–9.</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web|last=Federico|first=Ardila|date=2012|title=Matroids: Lecture 6|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=650w2Ufogwo|website=Youtube}}</ref>

:(B1) There is at least one base -- <math>\mathcal{B}</math> is nonempty;

:(B2) If <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> are distinct bases, and <math>a\in A\setminus B</math>, then there exists an element <math>b\in B\setminus A</math> such that <math>(A \setminus \{ a \}) \cup \{b\} </math> is a basis (this is the basis-exchange property).
(B2) implies that, given any two bases ''A'' and ''B'', we can transform ''A'' into ''B'' by a sequence of exchanges of a single element. In particular, this implies that all bases must have the same cardinality.

== Duality ==
If  <math>(E,\mathcal{B})</math> is a finite matroid, we can define the '''orthogonal''' or '''[[dual matroid]]'''  <math>(E,\mathcal{B}^*)</math> by calling a set a ''basis'' in  <math>\mathcal{B}^*
</math> if and only if its complement is in <math>\mathcal{B}</math>.  It can be verified that <math>(E,\mathcal{B}^*)</math> is indeed a matroid. The definition immediately implies that the dual of <math>(E,\mathcal{B}^*)</math> is ''<math>(E,\mathcal{B})</math>''.<ref name="Whi8632">{{citation|title=Theory of Matroids|url=https://archive.org/details/theoryofmatroids1986unse|volume=26|year=1986|editor-last=White|editor-first=Neil|series=Encyclopedia of Mathematics and its Applications|location=Cambridge|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-30937-0|zbl=0579.00001|url-access=registration}}</ref>{{Rp|32}}<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|last=Ardila|first=Federico|date=2012|title=Matroids lecture 7|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qBBe6XudNOQ&list=PL-XzhVrXIVeSu_b29hbX5xJ0bRThokU8a&index=7|website=Youtube}}</ref>

Using duality, one can prove that the property (B2) can be replaced by the following:<blockquote>(B2*) If <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> are distinct bases, and <math>b\in B\setminus A</math>, then there exists an element <math>a\in A\setminus B</math> such that <math>(A \setminus \{ a \}) \cup \{b\} </math> is a basis.</blockquote>

== Circuits ==
A dual notion to a basis is a '''circuit'''. A circuit in a matroid is a minimal dependent set—that is, a dependent set whose proper subsets are all independent.  The terminology arises because the circuits of [[graphic matroid]]s are cycles in the corresponding graphs.

One may define a matroid <math>M</math> to be a pair <math>(E,\mathcal{C})</math>, where <math>E</math> is the ground-set and <math>\mathcal{C}</math> is a collection of subsets of <math>E</math>, called "circuits", with the following properties:<ref name=":2" />
:(C1) The [[empty set]] is not a circuit;
:(C2) A proper subset of a circuit is not a circuit;
:(C3) If C<sub>1</sub> and C<sub>2</sub> are distinct circuits, and ''x'' is an element in their intersection, then <math>(C_1 \cup C_2) \setminus \{x\}</math> contains a circuit.

Another property of circuits is that, if a set <math>J</math> is independent, and the set <math>J \cup \{x\}</math> is dependent (i.e., adding the element <math>x</math> makes it dependent), then <math>J \cup \{x\}</math> contains a ''unique'' circuit <math>C(x,J)</math>, and it contains <math>x</math>. This circuit is called the '''fundamental circuit''' of <math>x</math> w.r.t. <math>J</math>. It is analogous to the linear algebra fact, that if adding a vector <math>x</math> to an independent vector set <math>J</math> makes it dependent, then there is a unique linear combination of elements of <math>J</math> that equals <math>x</math>.<ref name=":3" />

== See also ==

* [[Matroid polytope]] - a polytope in R''<sup>n</sup>'' (where ''n'' is the number of elements in the matroid), whose vertices are indicator vectors of the bases of the matroid.
